spans.text: The ferry came around the headland at twenty past four in the afternoon on a Sunday in the last week of August, on a sea that was a green he had only seen in his mother’s bathroom tile on Cavenagh Street, on a boat with a diesel smell at the back of his throat he had been at for thirty-six hours from Darwin.
He had not slept.

He had been awake on the eleven-hour Singapore-to-Athens flight, awake on the Athens-to-Kos connector, awake on the Kos-to-Pothia ferry for the full hour and a half because the deck rail was where he had decided at the Aegean Airlines gate in Athens he would be when the boat came around the headland.
The headland came at four eighteen.
The harbor came up on the left.
The harbor was a harbor.

His grandmother in Darwin had said in February, when he had first told her where he was going, that Pothia was not Kastellorizo. She had said it the way she said most things, which was once, in Greek, with the slow Kastellorizan vowels she had been carrying in her mouth for seventy-nine years. She had said Pothia was the place a Pothia man went to and that he should not go expecting Kastellorizo. He had not been to Kastellorizo either. She had not been to Kastellorizo since 1947. The two places were the two he had not been to. He had told her that. She had said go to Pothia.

He had not been told, until two months ago when his sister Sophia had texted him from Athens, that Sophia was going to be at Symi as a senior fellow for his Year 1. Sophia had not told the family until the program’s central office in Athens had confirmed her placement in June. Sophia had said in the text that she would tell their parents on a Sunday call the next week. She had. The family had absorbed it. His grandmother had said nothing for two days and had then said: Sophia at Symi. Niko at Pothia. The cousins-who-stayed in two boats. She had not said more.

His father had driven him to Darwin airport at one in the morning Saturday Darwin time. His father had not gotten out of the car at the curb. His father had nodded at him through the open passenger window and had said kori in the way he used the word for either of his children at the moment of being placed onto a thing, and had driven away.
His mother had cried at the front door before they had left. She had cried quietly. He had said Mama. She had said Niko. He had held her shoulders for a count of nine. She had let go.

His younger sister Theo at fourteen had been at the kitchen in her pyjamas with a slice of toast she had made for him. Theo had said: bring back a stone from the harbor and put it on my dresser. He had said: I will.

His grandmother had not been at the house at midnight. He had been at her flat the night before. She had given him a package wrapped in brown paper that he had not opened yet and that was in his suitcase tonight. She had said: open it when you are at the kitchen in Pothia, not before.

A dense Kalymnian town climbed the slope from the harbor to a kastro on the ridge. White-and-blue-and-faded-yellow houses. A parish church bell tower at the top. The late-August air carried the smell of warm stone and diesel and the sea on its still afternoon turn. The dock with the sponge boats his father had been supplying parts to for thirty-one years.
The boats were sponge boats.

His father supplied parts to sponge boats. His father had been at it for thirty-one years. His father had not been to Pothia. His father was a desk man with a phone at his ear. His son was at the deck rail of a ferry in Pothia at four eighteen on a Sunday in late August looking at a harbor full of sponge boats his family had been at one remove from for two generations.
The ferry came in to the dock at four twenty-five.
He picked up his bag.
He walked down the gangway.
A man was at the dock.

The man was at the bottom of the gangway with both hands in his pockets and the kind of stance Niko would later read as the Stelios stance, which was a stance in which Stelios had been at the dock for an hour because the program’s central office in Athens had told him on Friday that Niko was on the four-twenty Sunday ferry from Kos and Stelios had been there since three-twenty to be sure he had not misread the schedule.
Lekkas.
Vouvalis.
Niko.
Stelios.
You are jet-lagged.
I am thirty-six hours awake.
That is not jet-lag. That is something else.
Stelios took the bag.

Stelios was eighteen. He was a head shorter than Niko was. He had a face that had been at this dock for arrivals for two years already because Stelios had been the dorm assistant the previous summer and had now been promoted to local liaison for the new program intake. He had a steady walk. He did not introduce himself further. He said: we walk.
They walked.

The walk from the dock to the Drosos house was eight minutes. Niko did not register most of it. He registered the smell of the harbor at four-thirty in the afternoon, which was a smell of diesel and salt and sponge crates and something Greek-cooked at the kafenio at the corner of the harbor square. He registered three older men sitting outside the kafenio who looked at him without turning their heads. He registered an almond tree at the corner of two streets with a kind of late-August dust on it. He registered a bakery window on the right at half past four with the lights still on inside. The woman at the bakery counter looked up. The woman lifted her hand. Stelios lifted his. Niko did not.
My mother,
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: Stelios said.
She runs the bakery. You will be at the bakery in the mornings.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: All right.
spans.speaker: Niko

spans.text: Phaedon is at the dorm. Tia is at the dorm. Lina arrived Friday. The Tarpon Springs girl is on Wednesday’s ferry.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: All right.
spans.speaker: Niko

spans.text: You are the fourth.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: I am the fourth.
spans.speaker: Niko

spans.text: You have come the farthest.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: I have come the farthest.
spans.speaker: Niko

spans.text: He did not say more on the walk. Stelios did not either. The walk turned up a lane. The lane climbed a slope. The lane had a stone wall on the left that was the kind of wall Niko had been at in the photographs of Kastellorizo in his grandmother’s flat in Darwin, although he had not been to Kastellorizo and the lane was not Kastellorizo, and the wall was the kind of wall Greek islands had had since the eighteen-fifties.
The lane turned again.
The lane ended at a wide wood door.
The door was open.

The Drosos house at four-thirty-five was the kind of house his head had built. He had not known, before he had walked into the entrance hall, that his head had built the right kind of house, or that the seed had been a Pothia seed and not a Kastellorizan one. He stood at the threshold and let the not-knowing be on the other side of him.
The entrance hall had a photograph on the wall to the right.
He looked at the photograph.
The photograph was sepia. It was a family. The names were on a slip of paper behind the glass. The names were Eleni, Stamatis, Maria, Despina, Manolis, Markou Drosos. He read them.

He did not yet know any of them by their relation to anyone he had been near. He did not yet know in particular that he himself was a distant cousin to the Vouvalis-Markou cousin line, through a Maria who had been at this house at the kitchen for forty-five years, who had been his great-great-great-grandfather’s sister, the Lekkas-line connection his grandmother in Darwin had never named to him because she had never named it to herself.

He would learn that in Year 4 from a Spetses cohort-mate in Stuttgart’s textbook and a Tarpon Springs priest’s sister and a research letter from a Trieste-Italian-Greek scholar at the Cavenagh Street dorm in Darwin.
He did not know it now.
He looked at the photograph for a count of seven.
He turned. He followed Stelios.
The kitchen was at the back of the house.
Three of them were in it.

Phaedon was at the piano in the common room across the hallway with the lid up and one hand at a key, not playing, just holding the key down. He looked up when Stelios and Niko came past. He had a precise face and glasses on the table beside the piano. He did not stand. He nodded.
Lekkas.
Trakas.
Phaedon went back to the key.

Tia was in the kitchen at the long table peeling a bowl of garlic with a paring knife. She had her dark hair in a single braid. She had the kind of sweater Niko had only seen on Broome women at the Cavenagh Street markets in Darwin. She finished the garlic clove she was at. She set the knife down. She looked at him.
Lekkas.
Theodorakis-Coffin.
Broome to Darwin in nineteen-thirty-eight was fourteen hours.
By boat.
By boat. By Qantas in the eighties it was four. By road it is twenty-two now.
You have done it three times.
I have done it three times. You have done it two.
I have done it two.
She nodded.
She did not say more. She picked up the next garlic clove.
Stelios put Niko’s bag down at the kitchen door. Stelios said: Lina is upstairs. She will be down at five. The dinner is at seven. The dinner is for four. The fifth arrives Wednesday.
Niko nodded.
Stelios said: you will sleep at six. You will not sleep before. Sit at the table. Eat the bread. Drink the water. We will get you to bed at the right hour.
He nodded.
Stelios said something to Tia in Kalymniko Niko did not catch.
Tia answered in English. Tia said: I have the garlic.
Stelios nodded.
Stelios went to the hallway.
Niko sat at the long table.

The long table had been in this kitchen since 1898. The program had not replaced it. A scar marked the corner where he was sitting, made by a knife slipping in 1973. He did not yet know that. He saw the scar. He put his hand on it.
Tia put a piece of bread in front of him. Tia put a glass of water in front of him. Tia did not say more. She kept peeling.
He ate the bread.
Stelios’s mother had baked it that morning. She had been baking the Sunday loaves for forty-six years. He did not know that yet. He ate it.
It was good.
The water came from a well at the back of the courtyard the Drosos cooperative had drilled in 1894. He did not know that either. He drank it.
His head began to be the kind of jet-lagged head that did not know which way was twelve o’clock.
He did not say more.
He watched Tia at the garlic.
He watched the kitchen.

The kitchen had a window at the back that opened onto a courtyard. The courtyard had a wisteria over a stone table. The wisteria was at the end of its August flowering. The petals had been falling onto the stone for two weeks. The courtyard had a stone well at the back. The kitchen had a stove on the right wall and a sink on the left and a long countertop. The kitchen had a small clay bowl on the windowsill above the sink that he would later learn was the crumb bowl.
He had not been at a Pothia kitchen.
His great-great-great-grandmother Maria had been at this one as a girl in the eighteen-fifties. He did not know that yet.
He ate the bread.
Lina came down at five.
She was a sixteen-year-old with shoulder-length black hair and a notebook in her hand and a wisteria petal in her hair from the courtyard.
Niko.
Lina.
Bag in the front hall.
My bag is at the kitchen door.
Take it up. Second floor. The room at the top of the stairs. The harbor-side single.
All right.
You have not slept.
I have not slept.
You will sleep at six. You will eat at seven. You will be at the table for forty minutes. You will sleep again at nine.
All right.
I am Lina. I am from Sfax.
You are from Sfax.
You are from Darwin.
I am from Darwin.

My mother spent a week in Darwin in nineteen ninety-five at a teaching conference. She has a postcard on her dresser at home of the Cavenagh Street market. The postcard has been on her dresser for thirty-one years.
My mother has been at Cavenagh Street.
My mother does not know your mother. My mother does know the Cavenagh Street market.
All right.
All right.

She did not say more. She turned. She walked back upstairs. The fourth and ninth stairs creaked. He noted the creak. He did not yet know that Lina would learn to walk on the not-creaky pattern by mid-October and that he himself would learn the pattern by November.
He took his bag up.

The room at the top of the stairs was a single room. It had a bed against the inside wall. A dresser. A window that faced the harbor on the side that the room had been called the harbor-side single for. A writing desk. A pull-cord light fixture from the nineteen-sixties. Every Year-1 harbor-master intern had slept here since 2017, when Stelios had assigned the room to the role. It was Niko’s for the year.
He set the bag down on the floor.
He took his shoes off.
He did not unpack.
He lay down on the bed in his clothes.
He set his phone on the dresser.
He turned the phone face-down.
He did not turn it off.
He closed his eyes.
He slept at five-twelve in the afternoon Pothia time, which was twelve-twelve in the morning Darwin time, which was the kind of hour Niko at home in Darwin would never have been awake at.
He slept until six-forty-five.
The dinner was at the kitchen at seven.

Stelios had been at the bakery picking up the dinner bread at six. Phaedon had been at the kitchen counter cooking. Tia had been at the table laying out the plates. Lina had been at the doorway between the kitchen and the courtyard reading a book in French.
Niko came down at six fifty-five.

He had washed his face. He had drunk a glass of water at the bathroom sink. He had changed his shirt. He had brushed his hair the way his mother had taught him to brush his hair before dinner when he was six. He had been at the bedroom for an hour and forty minutes asleep and ten minutes awake. He was the kind of awake a jet-lagged seventeen-year-old was when he had slept ninety minutes after thirty-six hours and was facing dinner with three other seventeen-year-olds he had never met in person.
He sat at the chair Tia had set for him, which was the chair at the side of the table on the harbor-side, which was the chair that became his for the next two years.
He did not yet know it was his chair for the next two years. He sat in it.
Phaedon set a bowl of soup in front of him.

Fava bean soup with lemon and olive oil and fried onion on top. Phaedon had been cooking it on Sunday evenings since he was nine at his grandmother’s kitchen in Nea Smyrni. Niko did not yet know any of that.
He ate.
It was good.
The four of them ate without speaking for ten minutes.
The first to speak was Tia.
Tia said:
The American is on Wednesday.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Lina said:
Wednesday.
spans.speaker: Lina

spans.text: Phaedon said:
Wednesday at four-forty.
spans.speaker: Phaedon

spans.text: Niko said:
What is the American’s name.
spans.speaker: Niko

spans.text: Stelios said:
Athena Markou. Tarpon Springs, Florida.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: Tia said:
Tarpon Springs is a sponge town.
spans.speaker: Tia

spans.text: Niko said:
Tarpon Springs has been a sponge town for a hundred and twenty years. My father supplies parts to a Tarpon Springs cooperative.
spans.speaker: Niko

spans.text: Stelios said:

You will be at the cooperative office below the dorm with Mihalis the cooperative manager for the year. The cooperative office in Pothia has a Tarpon Springs file. The cooperative office in Tarpon Springs has a Pothia file. The Tarpon Springs file has had a Pothia letter on its top shelf since nineteen forty-eight that your father has not been at the bottom of.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: Niko looked at Stelios.
Stelios said:
I have read the program’s intake on you.
spans.speaker: Stelios

spans.text: You have read the program’s intake on me.

I have read it twice. The Lekkas family has been at Darwin since nineteen forty-seven. The Kastellorizo emigration. Your grandmother. The cooperative office at Pothia has a file from a nineteen forty-eight letter your great-grandfather sent the cooperative asking after a member of his Pothia line. The cooperative office had not replied. The cooperative office still has not replied. The file is on the top shelf in the back room. Mihalis told me about it in June. Mihalis told me you would not know.
I do not know.
You will know.
All right.
Stelios did not say more.
Lina did not say more.
Tia did not say more.
Phaedon did not say more.
The four of them ate the soup.
Niko did not register most of what Stelios had said. The Lekkas file. The 1948 letter. He registered it as a sentence at the table.
He finished his soup.
Phaedon brought out a plate of bread and cheese.
The four of them ate.
Stelios got up at seven-forty. He cleared the bowls. He set them in the sink. He did not wash them. He said: Niko sleeps. The rest of us are at the courtyard.
The three of them and Stelios went out.
Niko sat at the table for a count of forty.
He did not move.
He thought about Stelios’s Lekkas family at Darwin since nineteen forty-seven.

He thought about a file with a 1948 letter in it from his great-grandfather Kostas Lekkas asking after a Pothia line. He had been raised on a Kastellorizo story for sixteen years. There had been a Pothia story. The Pothia story had not been told to him. He thought of his grandmother in her flat in Darwin at midnight Darwin time, asleep, in the housedress she had been at the kitchen in for fifty years.

He did not yet decide what he thought about the not-telling. He decided he would think about it tomorrow. The disclosure his grandmother had been carrying was a year and three months away. He did not yet have its shape.
He stood up.

He took the bread crumbs from the table and put them in the clay bowl on the windowsill above the sink because Tia had told him on the way down to the soup that the bowl was for the crumbs and that the cat from the lane outside the courtyard came around in the morning.

He did not yet know that the cat was the cooperative cat that would be a cat for the duration of the program, that would be at the windowsill every morning for two years, that would be at the windowsill the morning Lina would put her phone on the kitchen table at six forty-five in March of Year 2.
He put the crumbs in the bowl.
He set the bowl on the windowsill.
He turned to the kitchen door.
Lina was at the door.
She had come back into the kitchen because she had been watching him through the courtyard window the whole time he had been at the table.
Niko.
Lina.
Sleep.
I am going up.
Niko.
Yes.

You are going to be at the kitchen at six in the morning. You are going to be jet-lagged at six in the morning. The kitchen is going to be at six in the morning. The bread will be at the bakery. Stelios’s mother will be at the bakery at five. The bread will be the morning bread. You will eat the bread.
All right.
Niko.
Yes.
What Stelios said about the cooperative file.
Yes.
You will go and find it.
I will go and find the file.

Not on your first week. Stelios said tonight because he had decided you should know on your first night that the file existed. The file has been on the shelf since nineteen forty-eight. The file will be there in October.
All right.
Lina.
Yes.
Why did you tell me that.

Because I read the way your face was at the table when Stelios said it. Your face needed to hear the part about October from somebody who was not Stelios. You needed somebody at the table at the start of the week and not at the end.
You are at the table.
I am at the table.
All right.
She did not say more. She did not move from the doorway. She had said what she had decided to say.
He nodded.
He went up the stairs.
The fourth and ninth stairs creaked. He registered the creak. He would later, in late October, learn to walk on the not-creaky pattern.
He did not register the pattern tonight.
He came to the bedroom. He closed the door. He brushed his teeth at the bathroom sink across the hall. He came back. He lay down on the bed.
He had been at the dorm for three hours.

The bed had been in this room since 1968, per Stelios’s email. The wall beside it carried no salt damage that he could see in the dim light from the corridor. He would learn in his first week that the room across the hall had a wall the harbor-side rooms had carried for ninety years. His was an interior wall.
His grandmother. Sophia at Symi. Theo at the kitchen at home, doing her homework on a Monday morning Darwin time. His mother and father asleep at three in the morning in Darwin.
The package wrapped in brown paper his grandmother had given him at her flat the night before. She had told him not to open it until he was at the kitchen in Pothia.
He had been at the kitchen in Pothia.
He had not opened the package.
He got up.
He went to the suitcase.
He opened the suitcase.
He took out the package wrapped in brown paper.
He sat on the bed.
He opened it.
The package had a single piece of folded paper in it.

The paper was a piece of stationery from his grandmother’s flat. The paper had his grandmother’s hand on it. Her hand on the paper was the hand he had been at her kitchen counter watching for sixteen years. The paper had three lines.
The lines were in Greek.
The first line said: Niko mou.
The second line said: The Pothia kitchen is the kitchen. Go to it. Do not come back to Darwin without going to it.
The third line said: I am sorry.
He read the lines three times.
He folded the paper.
He put the paper in the dresser drawer at the top.
He closed the drawer.
He did not yet know what his grandmother was sorry for. He would know in November of Year 3 at her flat. She had been carrying the apology since she was thirteen. He did not know it tonight.
He lay down on the bed.
He thought about the file on the top shelf in the cooperative office back room.
He thought about Lina at the doorway saying you needed somebody at the table at the start of the week.
He slept at nine-twelve in the evening Pothia time, which was four-twelve in the morning Darwin time.
He slept until the kitchen at six.
